mosfet-001.question: What is the condition for an enhancement-mode n-channel MOSFET to turn on (conduct)? (VGS: gate-source voltage, Vth: threshold voltage)
mosfet-001.explanation: In an enhancement-mode nMOSFET, a positive gate voltage above Vth draws electrons to the surface of the p-type substrate, forming an inversion layer (channel) so current flows between source and drain. At VGS = 0 V there is no channel and the device is off (normally off), which suits logic and makes power circuits fail safe. Vth is typically 0.2–0.4 V in advanced logic and about 1–4 V in power devices.

mosfet-002.question: If only the thickness of the gate insulator is reduced, without changing its material or area, what happens to the gate capacitance per unit area?
mosfet-002.explanation: The gate behaves like a parallel-plate capacitor with Cox = ε/t per unit area. Thinning the dielectric raises capacitance, so the same gate voltage induces more channel charge, increasing drive current and suppressing short-channel effects. But once SiO2 reached about 1.2 nm, tunneling leakage hit its limit, and from the 45 nm generation HfO2-based high-k dielectrics, which can be physically thicker, have been used.

mosfet-003.question: Why is the static (steady-state) power consumption of a CMOS inverter small?
choices: Because the supply voltage is high
Because current always flows into the gate
Because whether the input is 0 or 1, either the pMOS or the nMOS is off, so almost no current flows from supply to ground
mosfet-003.explanation: In a CMOS inverter, input 0 turns the pMOS on and nMOS off, and input 1 does the reverse, so in steady state there is always an off transistor between supply and ground and almost no through current flows. Power is consumed mainly by charging and discharging load capacitance during switching: P = α·C·V²·f. With scaling, however, off-state leakage has grown, and static power is no longer negligible in advanced chips.

mosfet-004.question: When a long-channel MOSFET operates in the saturation region, the drain current ID is roughly proportional to what? (VGS: gate-source voltage, Vth: threshold voltage)
mosfet-004.explanation: In saturation, a long-channel MOSFET follows ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)², so drain current is proportional to the square of (VGS − Vth) (the square law). VGS − Vth, the overdrive voltage, is a basic analog design parameter. In short-channel devices velocity saturation pushes the dependence toward linear, and mobility degradation and parasitic resistance add further deviations, so real designs use detailed models such as BSIM.

mosfet-005.question: For nMOS and pMOS transistors of the same size, the nMOS generally has a larger drive current. What is the main reason?
choices: The nMOS gate oxide is always thicker
A pMOS has no gate electrode
The mobility of electrons in the channel is higher than that of holes
mosfet-005.explanation: Electrons carry current in an nMOS and holes in a pMOS, and in silicon inversion layers electron mobility is about 2–3 times hole mobility, so an nMOS of the same size drives more current. CMOS balances this by widening the pMOS. In advanced processes, compressive strain from SiGe boosts pMOS mobility, and in FinFETs the fin sidewalls are (110) planes, which favor holes, so the gap has narrowed considerably.

mosfet-006.question: In an n-channel MOSFET, what happens to the threshold voltage when a negative voltage is applied to the substrate (body) relative to the source (body bias)?
mosfet-006.explanation: Reverse-biasing the source-to-body junction widens the depletion region under the gate and increases its charge, so a larger gate voltage is needed to compensate—the threshold voltage rises (the body effect). In stacked transistors the upper devices see raised source potentials, so their Vth increases and they slow down. Conversely, adjusting body voltage to tune Vth is used to cut leakage.

mosfet-007.question: Which is a characteristic of a depletion-mode MOSFET?
choices: A channel exists even at a gate voltage of 0 V, so current flows
No current flows even when the gate voltage is above the threshold voltage
mosfet-007.explanation: A depletion-mode MOSFET has a built-in channel and conducts even at 0 V gate voltage (normally on). For an n-channel device, a negative gate voltage removes the channel and stops the current. Early NMOS logic used them as load devices. Because they conduct when power is lost, they require safety considerations; GaN HEMTs are also inherently normally on, so special structures are used to make them normally off.

mosfet-008.question: Which value is closest to the theoretical lower limit of a MOSFET's subthreshold swing at room temperature (the gate voltage needed to change the drain current by one decade below threshold)?
mosfet-008.explanation: Below threshold, drain current still rises exponentially with gate voltage. The gate voltage needed to change it by a decade, the subthreshold swing S = (kT/q)·ln10·(1 + Cd/Cox), is about 60 mV/dec at room temperature even in the ideal case (Cd = 0). Every 60 mV of Vth reduction thus raises off-current tenfold, a wall that blocks further supply-voltage scaling. Devices such as tunnel FETs are being researched to beat this limit.

mosfet-009.question: How does a MOSFET behave in the linear region, where the drain-source voltage VDS is sufficiently small?
choices: Like a variable resistor whose resistance changes with gate voltage
Like a constant-current source independent of VDS
Like a diode that conducts in only one direction
mosfet-009.explanation: In the linear region drain current is nearly proportional to VDS, and the slope—conductance μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)—changes with gate voltage, so the device acts as a gate-controlled variable resistor. A switch's on state lies in this region, and on-resistance falls as gate voltage rises. The property is also used in analog switches and variable-gain circuits. When VDS exceeds VGS − Vth, the device enters saturation.

mosfet-010.question: What is the purpose of the LDD (lightly doped drain) structure in a MOSFET?
choices: To lower the resistance of the gate electrode
To lower the doping at the drain edge, relax the electric field, and suppress degradation by hot carriers
mosfet-010.explanation: The strong field near the drain creates hot carriers that are injected into the gate dielectric or create interface states, shifting threshold voltage and reducing current. An LDD structure uses the gate sidewall spacer to form a shallow, lightly doped region on the channel side of the drain, lowering the peak field and suppressing degradation. Today, more heavily doped shallow "extensions," which also help control short-channel effects, are the mainstream.

mosfet-011.question: In a MOSFET in saturation, what is the phenomenon in which raising the drain voltage shortens the effective channel length and slightly increases the drain current?
mosfet-011.explanation: In saturation, a pinch-off point forms where the channel vanishes at the drain end. Raising the drain voltage moves it toward the source, shortening the effective channel and slightly increasing drain current—channel-length modulation. It is modeled as ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)²(1 + λVDS) and sets the output resistance ro ≈ 1/(λID). Because shorter channels suffer more, analog circuits use longer L.

mosfet-012.question: What is the definition of the transconductance gm of a MOSFET?
choices: The ratio of the change in drain current to the change in gate voltage
The drain voltage divided by the drain current
The capacitance of the gate insulator
mosfet-012.explanation: Transconductance gm = ∂ID/∂VGS describes how much drain current changes per change in gate voltage. For a long-channel device in saturation, gm = 2ID/(VGS − Vth) = √(2μCox(W/L)ID). Amplifier voltage gain is gm × load resistance, and the intrinsic maximum gain is gm × ro. The gm per unit current (gm/ID) measures efficiency, and the gm/ID design method is increasingly used to size analog transistors.

mosfet-013.question: In a MOS structure on a p-type substrate, what is the state of the semiconductor surface when a negative voltage is applied to the gate?
choices: A complete vacuum with no carriers
mosfet-013.explanation: Applying a negative gate voltage to a MOS structure on p-type substrate draws majority holes to the surface—accumulation. A positive voltage first repels holes, leaving only fixed acceptor ions (depletion), and a larger voltage gathers minority electrons at the surface (inversion). These three states—accumulation, depletion and inversion—appear as capacitance changes in C-V measurements, a fundamental tool for evaluating MOS structures.

mosfet-014.question: Which design makes the logic threshold of a CMOS inverter about half the supply voltage?
choices: Set the supply voltage to 0 V
Make the pMOS gate wider than the nMOS so that their drive strengths are balanced
mosfet-014.explanation: Hole mobility is lower than electron mobility, so a pMOS of the same size is weaker and the switching threshold shifts toward ground. Making the pMOS 2–3 times wider than the nMOS balances drive strength, putting the threshold near half the supply, equalizing high and low noise margins and matching rise and fall delays. Wider pMOS adds area and input capacitance, so speed-critical designs sometimes use a smaller ratio deliberately.

mosfet-015.question: What is the advantage of a transmission gate, which connects an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel?
choices: It can pass both 0 and 1 without voltage loss
It can amplify the signal current
mosfet-015.explanation: A lone nMOS passes a 1 only up to VDD − Vth, and a lone pMOS passes a 0 only down to |Vth|. Placing them in parallel with complementary gate signals lets each cover the other's weakness, so both 0 and 1 pass without loss. Since signals can flow both ways, transmission gates are used in multiplexers, latches and analog switches (such as the 4066). They provide no drive, though, so long chains slow down and need buffers.

mosfet-016.question: What failure can occur when a voltage far above the rating is applied between the gate and source of a MOSFET?
choices: Dielectric breakdown of the gate insulator
mosfet-016.explanation: Gate dielectrics in advanced devices are only a few nm thick, and SiO2 breaks down at about 10 MV/cm, so a 2 nm film would fail at only a few volts. Breakdown shorts gate to channel and destroys the transistor. Static electricity (kilovolts) can easily cause it, so IC I/Os include ESD protection, and even power MOSFETs are rated around ±20 V gate-to-source. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) under prolonged voltage within ratings is also a reliability concern.

mosfet-017.question: What is the main reason the channel mobility of a MOSFET is lower than the mobility inside bulk silicon?
choices: Because the temperature in the channel is extremely low
Because carriers in the channel flow near the Si/SiO2 interface and are easily scattered by interface roughness and charges
Because the channel contains no impurities at all
mosfet-017.explanation: A MOSFET channel forms within a few nm of the gate-dielectric interface. Carriers are scattered by interface roughness, charges at the interface and in the dielectric, and phonons, and the stronger the gate field pulls them toward the interface, the more scattering they suffer, so mobility falls to about half of the bulk value or less. High-k films add remote-phonon scattering, so a thin SiO2 interlayer is kept at the interface to limit the mobility loss.

mosfet-018.question: In a short-channel MOSFET, what is the main reason the drain current falls below the (VGS − Vth) square law and approaches a linear dependence?
mosfet-018.explanation: As the channel shortens, the field within it strengthens and carriers reach their saturation velocity (about 1×10⁷ cm/s for electrons in silicon). Current then follows ID ≈ W·Cox·vsat·(VGS − Vth), nearly linear in (VGS − Vth). In this regime shorter gates no longer raise current as much as expected, so performance has been pushed by strain-enhanced mobility, higher gate capacitance and lower parasitic resistance.

mosfet-019.question: Which expression roughly represents the delay of a CMOS logic gate? (C: load capacitance, V: supply voltage, I: drive current)
mosfet-019.explanation: Gate delay can be viewed as the time for current I to charge or discharge load capacitance C to the supply voltage V, roughly CV/I. Scaling made circuits faster by shrinking C, but lowering V reduces I even more, so delay increases. The expression guides speed-up strategies—cutting wire capacitance, raising drive current, limiting fan-out—and is used to estimate ring-oscillator frequency.

mosfet-020.question: What is the sign of the threshold voltage (relative to the source) of an enhancement-mode p-channel MOSFET?
mosfet-020.explanation: In a pMOS, applying a gate voltage below the source forms a hole inversion layer at the surface of the n-type body (n-well), turning it on. An enhancement-mode pMOS therefore has a negative threshold voltage (e.g., −0.4 V). In circuits, with the source tied to VDD, it turns on when the gate is more than |Vth| below VDD. Design documents often compare magnitudes |Vth| to avoid sign confusion.

mosfet-021.question: What is the effect in which the gate-drain capacitance appears (1 + gain) times larger when seen from the input of an amplifier?
mosfet-021.explanation: In an inverting amplifier, the capacitor between input and output sees a voltage swing (1 + gain) times the input, so from the input it appears (1 + |Av|) times larger—the Miller effect, which for a MOSFET involves the gate-drain capacitance Cgd. The large input capacitance with the source resistance narrows bandwidth. Op-amp frequency compensation exploits the same effect, letting a small capacitor act like a large one.

mosfet-022.question: What problem results from depletion of the polysilicon on the gate electrode side of a polysilicon gate?
choices: It is equivalent to a thicker effective gate insulator, so drive current decreases
mosfet-022.explanation: Polysilicon is a semiconductor, so gate bias forms a depletion layer of about 0.3–0.5 nm on the gate-electrode side. It acts as a series capacitance, as if the dielectric were thicker, reducing drive current. As oxides thinned to around 1 nm this became significant. High-k/metal gate (HKMG) technology, from the 45 nm generation on, eliminated the problem by using metal electrodes.

mosfet-023.question: What is the general effect of lowering a MOSFET's threshold voltage?
choices: Drive current increases, but off-state leakage also increases
Both drive current and leakage decrease
mosfet-023.explanation: Lowering threshold voltage increases overdrive (VGS − Vth) and on-current at the same supply, but subthreshold behavior makes off-state leakage grow exponentially—about tenfold per 60–80 mV. Advanced processes therefore offer low-Vth (LVT), standard (SVT) and high-Vth (HVT) devices, and multi-Vth design uses low-Vth cells only on speed-critical paths.

mosfet-024.question: How are the transistors connected in a CMOS two-input NAND gate?
choices: Two pMOS in series and two nMOS in parallel
Two pMOS in parallel and two nMOS in series
mosfet-024.explanation: A NAND outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1, so the nMOS devices go in series between output and ground, connecting to 0 only when both are on, while the pMOS devices go in parallel to the supply, pulling high if either input is 0. Pull-up and pull-down networks being duals of each other is the basis of CMOS logic, and NOR is the reverse. Because series stacks are slow, NAND—which stacks the faster nMOS—outperforms NOR and is used more.

mosfet-025.question: Which phenomenon increases off-state leakage because band-to-band tunneling current flows due to the strong field where the gate overlaps the drain?
mosfet-025.explanation: Even when a transistor is off, a large gate-to-drain voltage bends the bands sharply near the drain edge of the gate, and band-to-band tunneling causes current to flow—GIDL, which notably grows as the gate is driven more negative. It is a problem in devices requiring ultra-low leakage such as DRAM cell transistors and is controlled by engineering the drain-edge doping and field. DIBL is threshold lowering by drain voltage, and NBTI is a pMOS degradation mechanism.

mosfet-026.question: What circuit advantage results from almost no current flowing into the gate of a MOSFET?
choices: A large DC current is needed to drive the gate
Switching speed no longer depends on gate capacitance
The input current is nearly zero, so almost no DC power is needed to hold a state
mosfet-026.explanation: Because a MOSFET's gate is insulated, essentially no DC input current is needed to hold its state. One output can therefore drive many gates, and CMOS circuits draw very little power when idle. This insulated gate is also what lets DRAM and flash retain charge. Charging and discharging gate capacitance still draws current at every transition, so drive power rises with frequency.

mosfet-027.question: Which is a characteristic of a MOSFET source follower (common-drain) circuit?
choices: Its voltage gain is slightly less than 1 and its output impedance is low
Its voltage gain is very large and its output is inverted
mosfet-027.explanation: In a source follower the source tracks the gate minus VGS, so the voltage gain is slightly below 1 (gmRs/(1 + gmRs)) and non-inverting; the body effect lowers it further. The input impedance is essentially infinite (it is a gate), and the output impedance is low, about 1/gm, so it serves as a buffer. It is the counterpart of the emitter follower, but its level shift (VGS) is larger than VBE and varies more.

mosfet-028.question: How does the absolute value of a MOSFET's threshold voltage generally change as temperature rises?
mosfet-028.explanation: As temperature rises, the Fermi level moves toward midgap and inversion becomes easier, so the threshold voltage magnitude falls by about 1–2 mV/°C. Mobility also drops, so the temperature dependence of drain current reverses with gate voltage, and at one bias point current is nearly temperature-independent (the zero-temperature-coefficient point). At high gate voltage mobility loss dominates and current falls; at low gate voltage the Vth drop dominates and leakage rises.

mosfet-029.question: How should the dimensions be changed to increase a MOSFET's drain current?
choices: Make the gate width W narrower and the gate length L longer
Dimensions do not affect drain current
Make the gate width W wider and the gate length L shorter
mosfet-029.explanation: Drain current is roughly proportional to W/L (gate width ÷ gate length). A wider gate widens the current path, and a shorter gate shortens the distance carriers travel, both increasing current. Widening W also increases gate capacitance and area proportionally. L is usually the minimum for the technology, but analog circuits use longer L to improve output resistance and matching. In FinFETs, effective width is set by the number of fins.

mosfet-030.question: Which combination lists the main components of leakage current in a MOSFET in the off state?
choices: Subthreshold leakage, gate leakage and junction leakage
No leakage current flows at all
mosfet-030.explanation: Even an off MOSFET leaks: subthreshold leakage below threshold, gate leakage through the dielectric, and junction leakage at the source/drain junctions (including GIDL). Each device leaks less than a nanoampere, but billions of them add up to watts in standby. Countermeasures combine high-k dielectrics, multiple threshold voltages, power gating of idle blocks, and body-bias control.

mosfet-031.question: What structure does the "MOS" in MOSFET stand for?
mosfet-031.explanation: MOS stands for Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor, describing the stack of gate electrode (metal), gate dielectric (oxide) and semiconductor substrate. From the 1970s the gate electrode was polysilicon, and from the 45 nm generation it became metal again with high-k dielectrics such as HfO2, but the name stuck. Emphasizing the insulated gate, it is also called a MISFET (Metal-Insulator-Semiconductor).
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a metal-oxide-semiconductor stack.
It is not an abbreviation for carrier types.
It is not an abbreviation for circuit functions.

mosfet-032.question: Besides the gate, source and drain, what is the fourth terminal of a MOSFET?
mosfet-032.explanation: A MOSFET is a four-terminal device: gate, source, drain, and the body (substrate or back gate) where the channel forms. Discrete parts tie the body to the source internally, so they look like three-terminal devices—which creates a parasitic body diode between source and drain. In ICs, the nMOS body is tied to the lowest potential and the pMOS body (n-well) to the highest so the junctions are never forward-biased.
choiceNotes: The emitter is a bipolar transistor terminal.
Correct. The fourth terminal is the body (substrate).
The collector is a bipolar transistor terminal.

mosfet-033.question: Which carriers carry the current in the channel of an n-channel MOSFET?
mosfet-033.explanation: In an n-channel MOSFET, the gate draws electrons to the surface of the p-type substrate to form an inversion layer, and those electrons carry current from source to drain (conventional current flows drain to source). The source and drain are heavily doped n+ regions that supply and collect the electrons. Electrons have higher mobility than holes, so an nMOS drives more current for its size, and most power MOSFETs are n-channel.
choiceNotes: Holes carry the current in a p-channel MOSFET.
Ions do not carry current in a MOSFET channel.
Correct. Electrons carry the current in an n-channel device.

mosfet-034.question: What does the "C" (complementary) in CMOS mean?
choices: Circuits are built only from nMOS transistors connected in series
nMOS and pMOS transistors are combined and operate in a complementary way
Bipolar transistors and MOSFETs are combined
mosfet-034.explanation: CMOS pairs nMOS and pMOS transistors. When the input changes, one turns on and the other off, so in steady state there is no path from supply to ground and power consumption stays low. The output swings fully to the supply and ground rails, giving large noise margins. Proposed in 1963, CMOS replaced power-hungry NMOS and bipolar logic as the LSI standard in the 1980s.
choiceNotes: Using only nMOS transistors is NMOS logic.
Correct. nMOS and pMOS are combined in a complementary way.
Combining bipolar transistors with CMOS is called BiCMOS.

mosfet-035.question: When a MOSFET is used as a switch, which statement correctly describes its on-resistance?
choices: The source-drain resistance when the device is off
The resistance of the gate electrode itself
The source-drain resistance when the device is on; the smaller it is, the lower the loss
mosfet-035.explanation: On-resistance RDS(on) is the drain-source resistance when the MOSFET conducts, and conduction loss is I²R—10 A through 10 mΩ dissipates 1 W. It decreases as gate voltage rises (more channel carriers) and increases with temperature (about 1.5× at 100 °C as a rule of thumb). In power MOSFETs, on-resistance rises steeply with voltage rating, so superjunction structures and SiC are used to break that trade-off.
choiceNotes: The resistance when off is very large and is not called on-resistance.
The resistance of the gate electrode is called gate resistance, a different thing.
Correct. It is the drain-source resistance while conducting.

mosfet-036.question: For a typical MOSFET in an integrated circuit, which statement about the source and drain is correct?
choices: The structure is nearly symmetric, and which side acts as the source depends on the potentials
The source always has a higher impurity concentration than the drain
The source and drain are made of different semiconductor materials
mosfet-036.explanation: In typical IC MOSFETs, the source and drain are identical diffusions made in the same step, so the device is essentially symmetric. In an nMOS, whichever terminal is at lower potential acts as the source, so current direction can reverse, as in transmission gates or DRAM cell transistors. Power MOSFETs and LDMOS, by contrast, are asymmetric, with a drain structure engineered for high voltage, and the terminals cannot be swapped.
choiceNotes: Correct. The structure is symmetric, and the potentials decide the roles.
In an ordinary MOSFET, the source and drain have the same doping.
The source and drain are made of the same material in the same process step.

mosfet-037.question: What is the condition for a long-channel nMOSFET to operate in the saturation region? (Assume VGS > Vth.)
mosfet-037.explanation: With VGS > Vth and a channel present, once VDS ≥ VGS − Vth the gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end falls below Vth, the channel pinches off, and drain current becomes nearly independent of VDS—the saturation region. Amplifiers operate here, and the minimum VDS (= VGS − Vth) sets the lower limit of output swing. In short-channel devices velocity saturation makes current saturate at a lower VDS.
choiceNotes: With VDS = 0, no current flows.
VDS < VGS − Vth is the condition for the linear region.
Correct. This is the condition for pinch-off at the drain end.

mosfet-038.question: How does the threshold voltage change when the impurity concentration of the channel region (p-type substrate) of an nMOSFET is increased?
mosfet-038.explanation: Higher substrate doping means more acceptor charge in the depletion region before the surface inverts, and a larger Fermi potential φF, so more gate voltage is needed and Vth rises. Channel implants adjust Vth this way. But heavy doping lowers mobility and increases variability from random dopant fluctuation, so FinFETs and GAA devices use nearly undoped channels and set Vth with the gate work function.
choiceNotes: Correct. More depletion charge must be overcome before inversion.
Lowering the concentration lowers the threshold; raising it does the opposite.
Substrate doping is one of the main factors that set the threshold voltage.

mosfet-039.question: If the gate insulator of an nMOSFET is made thicker with all else unchanged, how does the magnitude of the threshold voltage generally change?
mosfet-039.explanation: A thicker gate dielectric lowers Cox, so more gate voltage is needed to support the same depletion charge and the threshold magnitude increases (the Qd/Cox term in Vth = VFB + 2φF + Qd/Cox grows). Within one chip, thin-oxide transistors serve the core while thick-oxide transistors handle 1.8 V or 3.3 V I/O (dual gate oxide). Thick-oxide devices tolerate higher voltage but are slower and have higher Vth.
choiceNotes: Oxide thickness alone does not make the threshold voltage zero.
Correct. Cox decreases, so the required gate voltage rises.
A thinner insulator tends to reduce the threshold voltage.

mosfet-040.question: Which generally describes the relationship between a MOSFET's gate length (the length of the gate electrode on the mask or after patterning) and its effective channel length?
choices: The effective channel length is shorter than the gate length by the amount the source and drain extend laterally under the gate
The effective channel length is always longer than the gate length
The effective channel length always equals the gate length exactly
mosfet-040.explanation: Source/drain dopants spread laterally under the gate during implantation and annealing, so the effective channel length is shorter than the gate length by the overlap on each side. The overlap forms gate-to-source/drain overlap capacitance, which adds delay via the Miller effect. Advanced generations limit the spread with ultrafast (millisecond) anneals. Note that node names like "3 nm" do not correspond to actual gate lengths.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is shorter by the lateral extension (overlap).
Dopants extend under the gate, so the effective length gets shorter, not longer.
Because of lateral diffusion, they generally do not match.

mosfet-041.question: Which correctly describes punch-through in a MOSFET?
choices: A drop in channel mobility with temperature
The source and drain depletion layers merge and current flows that the gate cannot control
Dielectric breakdown of the gate insulator
mosfet-041.explanation: With a short channel and light substrate doping, the drain's depletion region can merge with the source's under drain bias, so current flows deep in the substrate independent of the gate and the device cannot turn off—punch-through. Remedies include heavily doped halo (pocket) implants beneath the source/drain, shallower junctions, and, as in FinFETs and GAA devices, wrapping the gate around the channel to eliminate uncontrolled paths.
choiceNotes: The temperature dependence of mobility is not punch-through.
Correct. The depletion layers merge and uncontrollable current flows.
Insulator breakdown is gate oxide breakdown, a different phenomenon.

mosfet-042.question: In a pass transistor (switch) made of a single nMOSFET with its gate at the supply voltage VDD, how high does the output rise when passing an input of VDD?
mosfet-042.explanation: An nMOS turns off when VGS drops below Vth, so as the output (source side) approaches VDD − Vth, current nearly stops and the output rises no further. The body effect raises Vth as the source potential climbs, so the actual level is a bit lower still. This weak 1 cannot fully turn off the next stage's pMOS, causing leakage. Since 0 passes fully, a transmission gate pairing the nMOS with a pMOS is used.
choiceNotes: Reaching VDD requires measures such as adding a pMOS in parallel.
The output cannot exceed the gate voltage.
Correct. It stops one threshold voltage below VDD.

mosfet-043.question: In a CMOS inverter, what is the current that flows from the supply to ground while the input is switching called?
mosfet-043.explanation: While the input passes through intermediate voltages, the nMOS and pMOS are both partly on and current flows directly from supply to ground—short-circuit (crowbar) current. Slower input transitions prolong it, so rise and fall times are kept short, and design tools insert buffers to meet maximum-transition limits. With fast transitions it stays at roughly a tenth of dynamic power or less.
choiceNotes: Gate leakage current is current through the gate insulator.
Correct. It flows while both transistors are on at the same time.
Subthreshold current is leakage in a transistor that is off.

mosfet-044.question: Power MOSFETs are easy to use in parallel. Which statement about the temperature dependence of on-resistance explains why?
choices: On-resistance falls as temperature rises, so current concentrates further in the hottest device
On-resistance rises with temperature, so a device that heats up naturally carries less current and the current spreads out
mosfet-044.explanation: A MOSFET's on-resistance increases with temperature because mobility drops (a positive temperature coefficient). If one of several paralleled devices heats up, its resistance rises and its current falls, shifting current to the others, so thermal runaway is unlikely and paralleling is easy. Near threshold, at low gate voltage, the coefficient turns negative, however, so linear-mode operation or slow switching can still cause current crowding.
choiceNotes: On-resistance changes considerably with temperature.
Resistance falling with temperature and concentrating current is the property behind thermal runaway in bipolar transistors.
Correct. The positive temperature coefficient naturally spreads the current.

mosfet-045.question: Under Dennard (constant-field) scaling, which statement is correct when dimensions and voltages are each scaled by 1/k?
choices: Circuit delay becomes 1/k, and power density stays constant
Circuit delay increases by a factor of k
Power density increases by a factor of k²
mosfet-045.explanation: Under Dennard (constant-field) scaling, shrinking dimensions and voltage by 1/k and raising doping by k keeps the field constant: delay falls to 1/k, per-device power to 1/k², and area to 1/k², so power density stays constant. Published in 1974, it guided scaling for nearly 30 years. From the mid-2000s, subthreshold leakage prevented further cuts in Vth and supply voltage, scaling broke down, clock frequencies stalled and the industry turned to multicore.
choiceNotes: Correct. Circuits get faster and power density stays constant.
Smaller dimensions reduce delay (make circuits faster).
Because voltage is also reduced, power density ideally stays constant.

mosfet-046.question: Which correctly describes the flat-band voltage of a MOS structure?
choices: The gate voltage at which the channel reaches strong inversion
The gate voltage at which the gate insulator breaks down
The gate voltage at which the bands at the semiconductor surface are not bent (are flat)
mosfet-046.explanation: The flat-band voltage VFB is the gate voltage at which the semiconductor's bands at the surface are flat, given by VFB = φms − Qox/Cox (work-function difference and charge in the dielectric and at the interface). Threshold voltage is VFB plus 2φF and the voltage from depletion charge. Shifts in VFB seen in C-V measurements reveal oxide charge and contamination such as Na ions, making it an important process-control metric.
choiceNotes: The voltage at strong inversion is the threshold voltage.
The voltage at which the insulator fails is the breakdown voltage.
Correct. It is the gate voltage at which the surface bands are flat.

mosfet-047.question: In a high-frequency C-V measurement of a MOS capacitor on a p-type substrate, what happens to the capacitance when a large positive gate voltage drives the surface into strong inversion?
choices: It stays nearly constant at its minimum value
It reaches a maximum equal to the oxide capacitance Cox
mosfet-047.explanation: At high frequency (typically 1 MHz), minority-carrier generation in the inversion layer cannot follow the signal, so the inversion layer does not contribute to the AC capacitance. Capacitance therefore stays near its minimum, set by Cox in series with the depletion capacitance at maximum depletion width. At low (quasi-static) frequency the inversion layer responds and capacitance returns to Cox. The ratio of minimum to maximum capacitance yields the substrate doping, a standard MOS characterization.
choiceNotes: Correct. At high frequency the inversion layer cannot follow, so the capacitance stays at its minimum.
The capacitance never becomes infinite.
It equals Cox in accumulation, or in inversion at low frequency.

mosfet-048.question: In a MOSFET with a very thin gate insulator, what is the effect of the electron distribution in the inversion layer peaking slightly away from the interface?
choices: The gate insulator appears effectively thicker, reducing gate capacitance (and drive current)
The gate insulator appears effectively thinner and the gate capacitance increases
mosfet-048.explanation: Electrons in the inversion layer are confined in a narrow well by the strong interface field, and quantum effects place their distribution peak about 1 nm inside rather than right at the interface. With the charge centroid set back, the dielectric acts as if it were about 0.3–0.4 nm thicker in SiO2 terms, reducing gate capacitance and drive current. Together with poly depletion, this makes the electrical thickness (CET) exceed the physical EOT, and it matters more as EOT shrinks.
choiceNotes: This effect does not make the threshold voltage zero.
Correct. The effective insulator thickness increases and the capacitance decreases.
The charge centroid moves away from the interface, so the insulator appears thicker.

mosfet-049.question: Which expression appropriately gives the small-signal output resistance ro of a MOSFET in saturation, using the channel-length modulation coefficient λ and drain current ID?
mosfet-049.explanation: Including channel-length modulation, saturation drain current rises slightly with VDS as ID(1 + λVDS), and the inverse of this slope is the output resistance ro ≈ 1/(λID). λ is roughly inversely proportional to channel length, so doubling L about doubles ro. The intrinsic gain gm·ro is only about 10–20 in highly scaled transistors, so cascodes and multistage designs are used to obtain enough gain.
choiceNotes: Correct. ro ≈ 1/(λID).
ID/λ has units of current times voltage, not resistance.
λ × ID has units of current per voltage, not resistance.

mosfet-050.question: Which is the common condition for "strong inversion" used to define the threshold voltage of a MOSFET? (φF: Fermi potential)
choices: The surface potential becomes 2φF (the surface minority carrier density equals the bulk majority carrier density)
mosfet-050.explanation: Strong inversion is conventionally defined as beginning when the surface potential reaches 2φF—that is, when the surface electron density equals the bulk hole density. The gate voltage at that point is the threshold voltage, Vth = VFB + 2φF + √(2εqNA·2φF)/Cox. In measurements, Vth is extracted by the constant-current method or by extrapolating the linear part of the ID-VG curve, so values differ slightly with the definition.
choiceNotes: A negative surface potential puts the surface of a p-type substrate into accumulation.
Correct. A surface potential of 2φF marks strong inversion.
Zero surface potential is the flat-band condition.
